title: First and Last Spot of a Value
statement:
You get a list nums sorted in non-decreasing order, which may contain repeats, and a number target.

Return [first, last]: the smallest and largest index where target appears. If it does not appear at all, return [-1, -1].

Your solution should run in O(log n) time.

examples.why: 5 would fit between 4 and 6, but it is not in the list.
Finding one 7 and walking outwards would cost O(n) here. Two separate searches stay O(log n).

constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: A plain binary search finds some index of the target, but not necessarily the first one. What should happen when you find a match?
When nums[mid] equals the target, do not stop. To find the first spot, keep searching to the left; to find the last, keep searching to the right.
Write one helper: the first index whose value is ≥ x. The first spot is helper(target); the last spot is helper(target + 1) − 1. Check that the first spot really holds the target.

explain.intuition:
Ask a cleaner question: "where is the first value that is at least x?" This is the boundary between a block of smaller values and a block of the rest, and binary search finds a boundary perfectly: look at the middle, and you always know which side the boundary is on.

The first spot of target is the boundary for x = target. The last spot is just before the boundary for x = target + 1, because that is where values bigger than the target start. If the first boundary does not hold the target (or is past the end), the target is missing.
steps: Write lowerBound(x): lo = 0, hi = n; while lo < hi, mid = (lo + hi) >> 1; if nums[mid] < x then lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid. Return lo.
pitfalls: Finding any match and then walking left and right. On a list of all equal values that is O(n).
Using hi = n − 1 with the half-open loop, which makes it impossible to report "past the end".

solutions.title: Linear scan
solutions.idea: Walk the list and remember the first and last index where the target appears.

solutions.title: Two lower-bound searches
solutions.idea: The first spot is the first index with value ≥ target. The last spot is one before the first index with value ≥ target + 1.

followups: Count how many times the target appears in O(log n).
The list is rotated at an unknown point. Can you still find the span in O(log n)?
